questions.problem:
According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field 
$F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}+1,\,{y}^{2}⟩$
across the triangle $C$ with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),$ and $(0,2)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14233578/assets/c3c617522488e6ebf47dd2b2a52c43a1fe06ccaef8cd1e8752ab4df5e2d4bd64.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}+1$ and $Q(x,y)={y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2(x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2(x+y).$

questions.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(-1,-2),(3,-2),$ and $(3,0),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{6}\,i-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14233578/assets/e1e4386f3cc75afb63823d74daa27b517e8e47d51fa08c5c9e5bf3ca6f3ca88c.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{6}$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{6},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 3,\,-2\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}{y}^{6}-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{0}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}({y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3},\,\sqrt[3]{x}+y⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14233578/assets/fa98f3db31860a463d0a551d5297895e61a6c041d852c04de04c44a194510961.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(3{x}^{2}y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{3}y+x)\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[((1)^{3}y+1)-((-1)^{3}y+(-1))]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2y+2)\,dy \\  & =[{y}^{2}+2y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =((2)^{2}+2(2))-0 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$
